title: Law of Mass Action and the Equilibrium Constant
subcategory: Equilibrium — Law of Mass Action, Kc, Kp, Reaction Quotient

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 11 — Equilibrium

summary: At chemical equilibrium, the ratio of product concentrations to reactant concentrations (each raised to its stoichiometric power) is a constant, Kc (or Kp for gases); comparing the reaction quotient Q to K at any point tells you which direction the reaction will shift to reach equilibrium.
explanation: The law of mass action (as refined into the modern equilibrium law) states that for a reversible reaction aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD at equilibrium, the ratio Kc = [C]^c[D]^d / [A]^a[B]^b is CONSTANT at a given temperature, regardless of the initial amounts of reactants/products used to reach that equilibrium state — Kc depends ONLY on temperature, not on initial concentrations, pressure (for a fixed temperature), or the presence of a catalyst (a catalyst speeds up the approach to equilibrium but does NOT change the equilibrium position or the value of K itself). For reactions involving gases, Kp (using partial pressures instead of concentrations) is often more convenient; Kp and Kc are related by Kp = Kc(RT)^Δn, where Δn is the change in moles of GAS (moles of gaseous products minus moles of gaseous reactants) — when Δn = 0, Kp = Kc exactly. The REACTION QUOTIENT Q has the exact same mathematical form as K, but uses concentrations/pressures at ANY given moment (not necessarily at equilibrium) — comparing Q to K tells you the direction a reaction will shift: if Q < K, the reaction proceeds FORWARD (more products form) to reach equilibrium; if Q > K, the reaction proceeds in REVERSE; if Q = K, the system is already at equilibrium with no net shift. A LARGE value of K (K >> 1) indicates the equilibrium lies far toward PRODUCTS (reaction goes nearly to completion); a SMALL value of K (K << 1) indicates equilibrium lies far toward REACTANTS (reaction barely proceeds forward) — this single number, once known, immediately tells you the general extent to which a reaction will proceed, without needing to solve the full equilibrium problem. Pure solids and pure liquids are NOT included in the equilibrium constant expression at all (their 'concentration'/activity is treated as a constant, effectively 1, since it doesn't meaningfully change during the reaction) — only gases and solutes in solution appear in the K expression, a very commonly tested simplification.
commonMisconceptions: Believing the equilibrium constant changes if you start with different initial amounts of reactants — K is a fixed value at a given TEMPERATURE only; different starting amounts will reach different equilibrium concentrations, but the RATIO (K) calculated from those equilibrium concentrations will always be the same.

Including pure solids or pure liquids in the equilibrium constant expression — these are correctly OMITTED from Kc/Kp expressions entirely, since their effective concentration/activity doesn't change during the reaction.

Assuming a catalyst changes the value of the equilibrium constant or shifts the equilibrium position — a catalyst only speeds up how QUICKLY equilibrium is reached (by lowering activation energy for both forward and reverse reactions equally), never changing the final equilibrium position or K value itself.
examples: For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ (Haber process), if Q calculated from current concentrations is less than the known Kc at that temperature, the reaction will proceed further in the forward direction to produce more ammonia.

A reaction with Kc = 10¹⁵ at a given temperature proceeds essentially to completion (equilibrium strongly favours products), while one with Kc = 10⁻¹⁵ barely proceeds forward at all (equilibrium strongly favours reactants).
genZNote: K doesn't care how you got there — same starting materials, different ratios, same K every time at that temperature.
